item.title: My interpretation of the Laws
item.content:encoded:
First off, loved the SCP. I have recently been digging deeper and deeper into the wiki and really enjoying what I've read. I've been reading the -001 proposals over the past couple days when I have downtime at work, and they're fantastic!

Anyway, exposition aside…

I believe that the Law of Blood represents natural order. The flow of life to death and back again, like blood in your body fuels and returns to be refueled.

The Law of Concrete then represents the rigidity of man-made order; swapping gnarling trees and cliff-sides for measured cities of right angles and human design.

That would leave the Law of Howling to be the inability for these two concepts to exist in tandem.

Therefore, the Law of Blood is the Scarlet King in his purest and most conceptual/ethereal form, the Law of Concrete is Man's conceptual fight against him, and the Law of Howling is actually what gives him form.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I will just say that this was very well executed. Your use of language (describing concepts by images and emotions instead of precise descriptions) was what kept me hooked to the end. The characters didn't feel forced or cliché and their interaction felt natural. I also liked the explanation of Procedure Montauk and its implications (Montauks recommendations to the 05)

However what bothers me the most is that in the end, Montauk was convinced by essentially a huge appeal to emotion. The entire conflict of this article is between the factual Researcher who always appeals to reason and the old man who always appeals to emotion. Why wasn't it pointed out that human emotion very well exists in a post modern society? You only need to look at a football match, a comment section or a wedding to see genuine emotion amongst people, and if I, an average reader can realise that why can't a senior researcher? Why does a man whose whole life was dedicated to facts and reason change his world view by someone essentially telling him "past good, present faceless and emotionless"?

I can see where you were going with the article and I will still upvote because asI said, its very interesting, but the ending kind of bugs me.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Exactly this.

I didn't find the children sympathetic at all, quite the opposite in fact, and as I read I kept getting confused as to what the main idea was. The hyperbolic children's vision of rape good, buildings bad, clashes a lot with the development of the article. I could see that they were supposed to be wrong due to their direct delight at violence, but then the article uses Montauk as the reader's surrogate to continue the narrative and he ends up joining the children. The article is basically saying that we are also supposed to see things his way by the end.

The conversations were always one sided, with Spivak being treated as the old wise sage, and Montauk as the naive uber-rational scientist that discovers the beauty of nature by the end. Even the final O5 message seems to paint them as not understanding "the truth" and ignoring Montauk's latest proposal and simply half-assing it because they don't "see the truth".

The entire thing is pointing to the children being correct, without any moment for the reader to realize that it's quite the opposite, by following an Avatar-esque outline to the letter.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Just because something is pedestrian philosophy doesn't mean someone isn't uncomfortably happy with having realised it.

If the children are ultimately a parody, ultimately as bad and bankrupt as you say, then it's an odd way of expressing it. They're proved to be correct over the course of the article, the audience POV character and avatar of the Foundation is convinced to join them.

This "parody" group is shown to be functionally infinitely powerful (or at least able to breach containment at will with the rifts) and morally correct enough to bring Montauk, a man who has been devoted enough to commit horrible acts and create procedure 110 in order to fight them and the King, over to their side. Robert's arguments fail at every point, and Spivak is the one who makes them fail. They win, and they win while showing that they're completely correct.
I can't really see any point where they're meant to be in any way negative, except of course because we know rape and murder are bad, but even then their arguments of "no really rape and murder are proper" are successful.

You didn't portray the children as sympathetic, you portrayed them as victorious and correct, or at least that's how it feels to me. I'm not saying you agree with them, because nobody except a few 4chan and Thulean Perspective weirdos think like that. I am saying that I dislike pretty much all the basic undercurrents and all I want to do after reading this article is feed Spivak into a woodchipper, except the article makes me think he'd escape somehow because he's always right.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
To add an opposing viewpoint, I feel that making the children sympathetic actually enhances the article and is what makes it great. Their views, while not something that you agree with, are something you can kind of understand and, if you squint a bit, almost believe are rational. And that's what I feel makes them frightening.

To me, the Scarlet King here represents that alluring desire to return to the "good old days" in face of the difficulties of the modern-day, despite the fact that the good old days we think of are actually just our own romanticized version. It feels so understandable because it is a real thing we often feel, even though we know it is wrong. It is this alluring and realistic horror that really makes me enjoy this article so much.

Making it more obvious that the children are just wrong I feel would kind of devalue the story into a simple "hey this is wrong", instead of making the reader think and allowing them to come to that conclusion (which at least I did).

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The good old "the olden days were more real" is as stupid now as when I first heard it.

I mean, that is rather the point of the skip.

This is my big regret about this one: not the postmodernism, which is so basis it probably shouldn't even be called postmodernism. If people think even the most pedestrian pseudo-postmodernism is "jerking it into my face" then I don't know what to tell them.

The problem is that I clearly made the children too sympathetic. They're meant to be a parody of nativist movements, movements trying to reclaim the past, movements who respond to the colonial or otherwise experience through a blend of traditionalist and modernist thinking: Fascism, Islamism, Hindu nationalism &c. But I wasn't explicit enough in saying that they're just as bad and bankrupt as the Foundation; I assumed that the content of their awfulness would overcome the way they're framed, but nope.

Still, every failure is a learning experience, hopefully I won't make this kind of mistake going forward.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
How to defeat the horrors of modernity, according to theorists of the French school: criticism of metanarratives, deconstruction, postcolonialism, new theories of sexuality and gender, overcoming the dominant signifiers.

How to defeat the horrors of modernity, according to Tufto: fuck each other with huge axes, slaughter villages, rape women, enslave peoples.

The author apparently read about Heidegger on Wikipedia or watched Dugin (lol) and, not knowing what to do with the revelation that fell on him, decided to write a 001. Let's have a closer look.

The past was brutal, but it was also real. It wasn't really the "premodern", too; that is merely how historians have characterized it. It is not clear that there has been a pattern that can be seen. It's all nonsense. As it really is.

Why was premodernism more real, why was modernism spoiled by harsh rationalism, and why did postmodernism mire in the virtuality of simulacra? Just because. The author does not explain, what is so real about fighting with huge blades. This must be taken as a given. It is clear that he most likely refers to the late Heidegger, or someone else, I do not know, but inside the article, not knowing about the references, it looks a little without proof and silly.

Montauk and the cultist guy behave like characters in scholastic dialogues. Here we have one scarecrow, which personifies the spirit the ratio of the enlightenment, and there is his critic, and now they will engage in a shallow commonplace dialogue.

And the funny thing is that this article just introduces a metaphysical, explanatory narrative, according to which the whole history of the Foundation is a struggle against the Scarlet King. This is so in the spirit of the western tradition, which loves to rationalize everything! Oh, irony!

Written well, especially the last spoiler, enjoyed that one very much. But in general, this is a bad article.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Just realized that I +1'ed this but I didn't comment it. So, I will do it now, with a simple answer to an usually complex (at least for me) question.

"Why I like this?"

I like this because I hate the SK. I hate the idea that someone could support him/it in real life. I hate what he stands for.
I hate the idea that the "premodern" may see the "modern" as wrong, only because we don't suffer life as they did.

+ show block
– hide block

We can discuss canon and headcanons as much as we like, but even in the universe of The Foundation the laws of physics exist.
Yeah, they can be fucked up by some SCPs and anomalies, but they still do apply to most of the world. In the same way, normalcy DOES exist, even if it isn't literal as anomalies exist.
What the Foundation stands for is the idea that we, humans, can understand things, and that we manipulate what we understand to do what we want, and this is in general to live a better life.

What makes me "hate" the SK and his followers is missing the point that this isn't hollow, not at all!
When we collect data and study things (or close monsters inside cages and fight against them) we aren't defining things, we are just observing them.
And from this observation actions take place.
AKA, rather than moving before thinking, modernity thinks before moving.
Why should this be hollow? Nobody "created" this behaviour out of thin air, it's a result of our evolution as a species. This is just another set of rules through which we play the same game.

The Foundation tries to be cold and distant, but in reality the Foundation is human to its deepest core, at least IMO.
It is based on the love for Life, which is extremely human. Protecting this reality we live in isn't the objective of the Foundation, it's just a way to protect humanity as a whole, to protect it from the dangers that lurks everywhere. It is human to fight for our lives. The Foundation just does it on a bigger level.
Love for Life is maybe the most human thing of them all, more than rage, sadness, pain and pleasure and whatever.

Yes, the world we live can be grey and slow and methodical, but then, what's wrong with that? How is a life of suffering and ignorance more "true" that this?
Humans are nothing more than animals evolved enough to understand the world around them a bit deeper than your average animal. All we did is completely in our nature, there is nothing "artificial" in it. As said before, we EVOLVED into this, we weren't made like this by something. It is in our nature to be like this. Denying this is denying our entire history. And I think that this is a lack of respect for the humans that came before us.
But also, the Foundation/modernity should remain true to its origins. We are nothing more than animals, and so emotions are part of us, denying that animal part of us it's useless.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

So yeah, I like this proposal (my favourite, probably surpassed only by Dr. Bright's one) because I truly hate it. It's written so good that I can hate it unironically.
In the SCPverse I wouldn't mind at all to work for real for something like the Foundation.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I feel you may have misunderstood a couple of things about the article (which I am sure is due to my own poor communication throughout).

Premodernity is not meant to "be" the tyrannical actions of the SK. The SK's tyrannical actions are an alteration to a premodern past by a premodernity in the process of being destroyed by modernity. They're explicitly not how things were in the premodern world, but are are rewrite of history performed by a dying premodernity in a world where the premodern is explicitly analysed by the modern. It's people trying to reclaim premodernity based on what they think predmodernity is, essentially: a stereotypical "dark ages".

The three quotes you reference are all about this in context. The first two were written by someone explicitly living through this re-write; the latter was by a modern-day follower of the SK describing this. This is a postmodern skip explicitly commenting (in that aspect) on how we, as moderns, percieve the premodern past, the alienation people feel within the modern ideologies which have replaced it, and the fact that people attempting to reclaim that premodernity end up promoting a twisted shadow of it, serving more as a reaction to what is than a reclamation of what was.

The Lala Raja document spells this out here:

+ show block
– hide block

Because what is he but the cry for a forgotten age? He is the British peasant staring up at the red sky, the Bengali widow's weeping and shaven head, the Aztec priest ripping out another's heart. He is all of those things transformed, as modernity does to everything, into modernity's own destruction. He is the resistance, the fury, the hatred of all that was for all that presently is.

What we were was full of good and evil and all else mixed together. The happiness, the beauty of the world, the struggles and heartache and reality of it all. But now we have lost almost all of it to the machine- except our rage. That's all that's left. And thus comes the King. The howl of the destroyed and forgotten and oppressed. His only purpose is to destroy, rape, maim, enslave and smile, smile that smile of a king whose enemies weep before him.

He cannot exist where there is no modernity, because his entire purpose is given to him by modernity. He is a god of blood, a god of spine and bone and sinew, to remind the denizens of this world that it is not good. It is cruel and hateful and that is good, that is right. Modernity is a sin and he is the correction, so that we can once again live as we must: cold, and hungry, and starving, and very, very afraid.

Long post collapsed. ~Zyn

I'm not sure I understand your point about pre-civilised and civilised life, as neither of those things are relevant to the article; those are not at all the same as modernity/premodernity.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like the ideas here, I really do, but they undermine themselves.

The Scarlet King is supposed to be pre-modern. Looking through the article, that apparently means something in a state of tyranny and nature, based in violence and fear.

The fortress was monumental, made of volcanic rock and jagged iron and built into a vast mountain. Every measurement, every angle was calculated to promote the King's ideology.

He rewarded us, and so we were the instruments of his rule. When a village required the justice of the King, we would descend upon them with blood and iron.

It is the way the Scarlet King ruled. There was order, but it was through the imposition of an iron will on the peasantry, through armies of slaves, through a nobility bred to be cruel.

None of these ideas or concepts are premodern.
Mathematics, mass construction efforts, religious and social hierarchy, and strict caste systems are all hallmarks of civilization and civilized life.
Human hunter-gatherer groups are extremely egalitarian in comparison to chimpanzees, for instance. Meta-analyses of time and work studies show that non-agricultural societies spend less time at work than industrial ones.

All humanity exists for the perpetuation of humanity. Civilization is a human construction made to further that purpose. This world is what we make of it.
Every farm, every citadel, every tyrant rests their power on their promise of safety. There is no distinction between the premodern and the modern, no dividing line. Civilization is a natural response, an adapative response, to the challenges of existence.

item.content:encoded:
The short of it is that the Scarlet King isn't exactly a "being". It's more of a concept.

But it became a being because the SCP shaped it to be so.

The Scarlet King is chaos. That's the law of blood.

But the modern world, especially the SCP Foundation, despises chaos. The Foundation wants to have everything well structured, reliable, understood. The more they try to understand the Scarlet King, the more they mold it into a real thing. This is the law of concrete.

There's an inherent conflict in this. The mold that the Foundation builds as they try to scientifically classify the Scarlet King is constantly being tested and pushed by the chaos that resides within. This is the law of howling.

item.title: My personal take
item.content:encoded:
I think I finally realized what the scarlet king is, and why I like this article. So, here's my interpretation:

+ my take
- my take

The scarlet king isn’t the premodern at all, or the postmodern even; it’s the fear of the premodern by the postmodern. The Foundation, in terror of what they perceived to be an assault on the normal, their structure and stability, created a false god by “filling” that mold (the law of concrete) with the law of blood (fear of the premodern and scariest of all to them, the idea that the postmodern has no inherent worth over the premodern), with the law of howling being this manufactured struggle based on that fear.

The Scarlet King cult exploits this fear by not only convincing people like Montauk that the fear and the violence that results is good, but also by exploiting the idea that this struggle itself is a necessary part of reality. Additionally, that line about how the Scarlet King didn’t exist before the Foundation makes me think that this fear isn’t just based around the premodern and postmodern, but how the Foundation interacts with that concept.

Ie. The Scarlet King is the idea that there can be no coexistence between the premodern and the postmodern.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Is this inspired by Howl, by any chance?

This article just doesn't quite cohere for me. I like most of the pieces you're building it out of, but they're not fitting together into a unified whole in my head. Here are a couple of them:

  • The lampshading of the Scarlet King's image (I liked "Always the same: […] the thing behind the eyes?" a lot), and the idea that this image is a retcon.
  • The concept of the Scarlet King as an equal and opposite reaction to Howl's Moloch.
  • The backstory for 110-Montauk.
  • The connection between the King and O5 decisions.

While typing up this list, I started to see more of a connection, but it still feels incomplete and not quite consistent to me.

EDIT: Here's a pair of more-concrete examples of things that seem contradictory or inexplicable to me.

  • Dipesh makes reference to "the King's sealing", even though the King as a force which could be sealed is supposed to have been the product of issues that arose much later.
  • It's supposedly Montauk's intent to be cruel that makes 110 effective, but that kind of motive seems like it should be something that acts in service of the King.
